title: Binary Search
relevance: Interviewers use it to test recognition of sorted or monotonic spaces and the ability to abstract a problem into a feasibility predicate that flips once.

phases.goal: Establish that binary search works on a sorted or monotonic space via an invariant that keeps the answer in [lo, hi] while halving the window.

must_hit.point: Binary search operates on a sorted or monotonic space to locate a target in logarithmic time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states sorted/monotonic input and log-time search by repeatedly discarding half the space.

must_hit.point: A robust template keeps the invariant that the target always exists within the search window [lo, hi], evaluates a midpoint, and halves the space while maintaining that invariant.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes an inclusive window and that each step shrinks it without breaking the invariant.

must_hit.point: The same template extends to boundaries: lower bound is the first element ≥ target and upper bound is the first element > target, mapping to std::lower_bound and std::upper_bound.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate distinguishes first ≥ vs first > and names the STL equivalents.

probes: When does binary search apply, and what invariant should your loop maintain?
What are lower bound and upper bound, and how do they differ from an exact-match search?

hints.1: Think about what property of the search space lets you safely discard half of it.
hints.2: Frame the loop as: answer stays in [lo, hi]; mid decides which side to keep.
hints.3: Lower bound = first ≥ target; upper bound = first > target; both reuse the same invariant-based window.

phases.goal: Show correct midpoint, exact-match and boundary updates, rotated-array half identification, and the isValid(mid) answer-space pattern.

must_hit.point: Always compute the midpoint with the overflow-safe formula int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2, not (lo + hi) / 2.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate writes or states lo + (hi - lo) / 2 and explains overflow risk of lo + hi.

must_hit.point: For exact match on a sorted array: if nums[mid] < target set lo = mid + 1; if greater set hi = mid - 1; return -1 when the window is exhausted.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate uses lo = mid + 1 / hi = mid - 1 and returns -1 when not found.

must_hit.point: For lower bound, initialize ans to the array size; when arr[mid] ≥ target record ans = mid and search left with hi = mid - 1; otherwise lo = mid + 1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate tracks a candidate index, moves left on ≥ target, and may return the array size if all elements are smaller.

must_hit.point: In a rotated sorted array with distinct values, at any midpoint at least one half (lo..mid or mid..hi) is strictly sorted; identify that half and check whether the target lies in its bounds.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate checks which half is sorted via endpoint comparison, then decides keep vs discard using target range.

must_hit.point: Binary search on answers separates search from feasibility: write bool isValid(mid) and binary-search the numeric range for the boundary where isValid flips from false to true.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes searching a value range and testing mid with a monotonic predicate helper.

probes: Walk through the exact-match and lower-bound templates—how do the boundary updates differ?
In a rotated sorted array, how do you decide which half to discard?
How do you structure binary search on the answer space for something like Koko eating bananas?

hints.1: Focus on what you assign to lo and hi after comparing mid—off-by-one here is the usual bug.
hints.2: Exact match discards mid; lower/upper bound records a feasible mid then continues toward the boundary.
hints.3: Rotated: one half is sorted—test target against that half’s endpoints. Answer-space: binary-search k/day/capacity and use isValid(mid).

phases.goal: Contrast linear vs logarithmic search, distinct vs duplicate rotated arrays, and flattened vs staircase 2D search.

must_hit.point: On a sorted array, linear scan is O(n) while binary search is O(log n) time and O(1) extra space for the basic templates.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts scanning every element with halving, and notes constant auxiliary space.

must_hit.point: Search in rotated sorted array with distinct values stays O(log n); with duplicates, when nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi] you must shrink lo++ and hi--, and the worst case is O(n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains the ambiguous triple-equal case and the average O(log n) / worst-case O(n) split.

must_hit.point: For a row-and-column-sorted matrix that is not globally flattened-sorted, per-row binary search is O(M log N) while staircase search from a corner is O(M + N).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts row-wise binary searches with eliminating a row or column each step in O(M + N).

probes: How do duplicates change complexity for search in a rotated sorted array?
For Search a 2D Matrix II, when would you prefer staircase search over binary search per row?

hints.1: Ask what you can still prove about a half when endpoint values are equal.
hints.2: Distinct rotated halves always give a sorted side; duplicates can make both sides ambiguous.
hints.3: Staircase from top-right eliminates a full row or column per step for O(M + N); per-row lower_bound is O(M log N).

phases.goal: Apply boundary templates and answer-space binary search to classic array, allocation, and 2D problems.

must_hit.point: Search insert position is exactly lower bound: the first index where the element is ≥ target (insertion point if absent).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate equates the problem to lower bound without a separate exact-match path.

must_hit.point: First and last occurrence use two binary searches (move left on match for first, move right for last); count of occurrences is last - first + 1, or 0 if absent.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate runs two boundary searches and derives count from the endpoints.

must_hit.point: Minimize-maximum / maximize-minimum problems (Koko, bouquets, ship capacity, aggressive cows, book allocation, split array) binary-search the answer and greedily test feasibility.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names the min-max/max-min signal, states the answer range, and describes a greedy isValid check.

must_hit.point: Median of two sorted arrays binary-searches the partition index on the smaller array so left halves total (m + n + 1) / 2 elements, validating cross bounds between left maxes and right mins.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate searches the smaller array, sets j from the half-size formula, and checks left1 ≤ right2 and left2 ≤ right1.

probes: How would you find the first and last position of a target in a sorted array with duplicates?
You need to minimize the maximum load across contiguous allocations—what’s the pattern?
How do you find the median of two sorted arrays in better than linear time?

hints.1: Boundaries and answer ranges are often the same template with a different predicate.
hints.2: For occurrences: lower-bound style for first, symmetric rightward search for last. For allocation: search pages/capacity/distance and greedily count groups.
hints.3: Partition the smaller array; j = (m+n+1)/2 - i; accept when left maxes ≤ opposite right mins.

tradeoffs.topic: Linear scan vs binary search on a sorted array
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Linear is O(n); because the array is sorted you can discard half each step for O(log n) time and O(1) space with a few index variables.

tradeoffs.topic: Exact-match template vs boundary (lower/upper bound) template
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Exact match returns mid on equality and shrinks with lo = mid + 1 or hi = mid - 1. Boundaries keep a candidate ans (often initialized to array size), update when the predicate holds, and continue toward the first feasible index—pick one of each and stay consistent.

tradeoffs.topic: Rotated search with distinct values vs with duplicates
tradeoffs.strong_answer: With distinct values, one half is always sorted and you discard a half each step in O(log n). With duplicates, nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi] blocks that test, so you shrink lo++/hi--; average O(log n), worst case O(n).

tradeoffs.topic: Flattened binary search (2D Matrix I) vs staircase search (2D Matrix II)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: If each row starts after the previous row ends, flatten to size M × N and search in O(log (M × N)) via row = mid / N, col = mid % N. If only rows and columns are sorted independently, flatten is invalid; staircase from a corner yields O(M + N), better than O(M log N) per-row searches.

tradeoffs.topic: Binary search on indices vs binary search on the answer space
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Index search probes array elements. Answer-space search probes a numeric range when feasibility is monotonic (if x works, larger/smaller values also work), using isValid(mid) to find the boundary—standard for minimize-max / maximize-min.

gotchas.trap: Writing int mid = (lo + hi) / 2 when lo and hi are large
gotchas.correction: That sum can overflow to a negative midpoint and crash; always use int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2.

gotchas.trap: Off-by-one boundary updates such as lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1
gotchas.correction: Almost every binary search bug is an off-by-one that can infinite-loop; pick one exact-match and one boundary template and apply them consistently.

gotchas.trap: Assuming nums[lo] <= nums[mid] proves the left half is sorted when duplicates exist
gotchas.correction: If nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi], neither half is identifiable (e.g. [3, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3]); shrink with lo++ and hi-- until the ambiguity clears.

gotchas.trap: Computing mid * mid directly when finding floor square root
gotchas.correction: mid * mid can overflow; use a wider type (e.g. long long) or compare with mid <= n / mid.

gotchas.trap: Treating a row-and-column-sorted matrix as a single flattened sorted array
gotchas.correction: That flatten trick needs each row’s first element greater than the previous row’s last; otherwise use staircase elimination or per-row binary search.
